newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Senior IMF official to meet Romanian leaders.
newsitem.headline: Senior IMF official to meet Romanian leaders.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund, which has suspended credits to Romania, is sending a top official to Bucharest this week to meet newly-elected President Emil Constantinescu, the Fund's representative said on Tuesday.

He said Poul Thomsen, the IMF's negotiator with Romania, would arrive on Wednesday with the aim of getting to know the reformist president who ousted ex-communists in elections. He also hoped to meet ministers of the government to be appointed within days.

"This is essentially a courtesy call to determine when the government will be ready to receive a team which could be put in the field quickly," resident representative Jonathan Hill said by telephone.

"You might call this a kick-off, a way to get acquainted. The programme of credits is basically non-operational and a decision has to be taken on how to proceed -- to launch a new programme or revive the existing one."
The central bank and officials connected with the new government hope the election outcome will improve Romania's image abroad and prompt the IMF to restore the credits quickly.
The IMF this year suspended a three-year standby credit programme of $460 million, the third agreed with post-communist Romania, with about two-thirds of the sum undistributed.

The Fund said the administration of defeated president Ion Iliescu, a former communist, had failed to observe agreements by allowing deviations in the foreign exchange markets by trying to prop the leu currency.
It also criticised government expenditure in an election year which pushed the budget deficit off target. "Basically, you can say that the programme went off track in 1996," Hill said.

The government, made up of Constantinescu's centrist Democratic Convention, Social Democrats and representatives of the 1.6 million Hungarian minority, is to present short and long-term economic programmes to parliament this week.
The Convention's electoral programme calls for budget discipline tempered by increased benefits for the needy.

Convention politicians have told local media that the new government will try to persuade the IMF to adopt a more flexible position over the next six months to liberalise exchange markets and eliminate subsidies to industry.
